name: Gnosticism
info: Gnosticism is a modern scholarly name for diverse religious systems that took shape by the mid-2nd century in the Mediterranean and Near East, centred on saving knowledge (gnosis) and a flawed creator; Mandaeism is counted as its surviving form.

facts.origin: the Mediterranean world, with Alexandria central to its birth; the origins cannot be traced exactly and are disputed, and the systems were fully developed by the mid-2nd century
facts.founder: none: a collection of groups and teachers, among them Valentinus (c. 100 – c. 180), Basilides of Alexandria and Marcion, rather than one founder
facts.scriptures: the Nag Hammadi library of 1945, with fifty-two mostly Gnostic treatises in Coptic, including the Gospel of Thomas and the Apocryphon of John; the Mandaean Ginza Rabba; and the reports of Church Fathers such as Irenaeus
facts.followers: Mandaeans, thought to number 60,000 to 70,000 worldwide, in Iraq, Iran and diaspora communities, and small modern Gnostic churches

t: Gnostic groups held that a hidden supreme being stood above a flawed creator, the demiurge, and that salvation came through direct knowledge (gnosis) of one's own divine origin.
For centuries it was known mainly through the hostile writings of Church Fathers such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus, until the Nag Hammadi library was found in Egypt in 1945.
Scholars now debate whether "Gnosticism" is a form of early Christianity, a category created by its opponents or a tradition in its own right, and many question its use as a single label.
dyk: The Nag Hammadi library, twelve leather-bound papyrus codices sealed in a jar, was found in 1945 by a local farmer, Muhammed al-Samman, and may have belonged to a nearby Pachomian monastery.
ev: Marcion of Sinope preaches in Rome, is expelled and starts a congregation that spreads through the Mediterranean
Irenaeus writes Against Heresies (c. 180–185), which names Simon Magus as the inceptor of Gnosticism
Mani travels to the Indo-Greek Kingdom of the Sakas in what is now Afghanistan (240–241), before joining the court of Shapur I
Bishop Athanasius condemns the use of non-canonical books in his Festal Letter, after which the Nag Hammadi codices may have been buried
Manichaeism becomes the state religion of the Uyghur Khaganate
The Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) begins; it and conversion to Islam greatly reduced the remaining Gnostics of the Middle Ages
Jules Doinel re-establishes a Gnostic church in France
The Nag Hammadi library is found near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt

sections.origins:
The origins of Gnosticism are obscure and disputed. Gnostic writings flourished among certain Christian groups in the Mediterranean during the 2nd century, and Alexandria is described as central to its birth. Scholars give several accounts of where it came from. Simone Pétrement and David Brakke argue that it arose as an intra-Christian movement, Pétrement tracing it to tendencies in the letters of Paul and the Gospel of John. Others, among them Gershom Scholem and Gilles Quispel, hold that it arose within Judaism, drawing on merkabah mysticism, and Quispel saw it as an independent Jewish development among Alexandrian Jews.

Earlier scholars proposed Persian origins, as Wilhelm Bousset and Richard Reitzenstein did, but Carsten Colpe showed many of Reitzenstein's hypotheses to be untenable. Others point to Middle Platonism, and a small minority see roots in Buddhism, though modern scholarship does not support Buddhist influence on Valentinus or the Nag Hammadi texts. Some scholars use "gnosis" for 1st-century ideas and keep "Gnosticism" for the synthesis of the 2nd century. According to James M. Robinson, no Gnostic text clearly predates Christianity. The term itself does not appear in ancient sources: Henry More coined it in the 17th century, from the Greek gnostikos that Irenaeus used about 185 for the school of Valentinus.
sections.beliefs:
Gnostic worldviews typically distinguished a hidden, uncorrupted supreme being from an inherently corrupt or flawed demiurge, who was responsible for creating material reality. In the Syrian–Egyptian traditions the supreme Godhead, the Monad, is remote. Lower divine beings, the aeons, emanate from it and together make up the pleroma, the region of light. The last of them, Sophia, gives rise to the demiurge, who is also called Yaldabaoth, Saklas or Samael, and who creates the material world and the archons that preside over it. Divine elements fall into the material realm and are latent in human beings, and redemption comes when they obtain gnosis, esoteric or intuitive knowledge of the divine. Many texts speak not of sin and repentance but of ignorance, illusion and enlightenment.

Gnostics tended towards asceticism, especially in sexual and dietary practice, and held that internal motivation mattered more than ritual. Views of materiality ranged from inherently evil to merely flawed, and of Jesus from an emanation of the supreme being who descended to bring gnosis to others, to a human mystic who attained enlightenment. Among the Mandaeans, Jesus was considered a false messiah. Manichaeism is called a radical dualism of two coequal forces, against the mitigated dualism of the classic Gnostic movements.
sections.texts:
Until 1945 Gnosticism was known mainly from the Church Fathers who opposed it, and their writings had an antagonistic bias and were incomplete. Justin Martyr criticised Simon Magus, Menander and Marcion in his First Apology. Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies about 180 to 185. Hippolytus wrote a ten-volume Refutation of all Heresies, of which eight volumes have been found, and Tertullian of Carthage wrote Against the Valentinians about 206. Several of these writers made little effort to record exactly the sects they described.

The Nag Hammadi library, found near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945, holds twelve papyrus codices with fifty-two mostly Gnostic treatises, three works from the Corpus Hermeticum and a partial translation of Plato's Republic. The original language was probably Greek and the codices are in Coptic. A 1st- or 2nd-century date has been proposed for the lost Greek originals, though this is disputed, and the manuscripts date from the 3rd and 4th centuries. The Apocryphon of John, the oldest text certainly known to be Gnostic, dates from the mid-2nd century. The Gospel of Thomas has many sayings parallel to the canonical gospels; Helmut Koester holds that its sayings are older, while John P. Meier reports that scholars predominantly conclude that it depends on or parallels the Synoptic Gospels. The Mandaeans keep their own scriptures in Mandaic, chiefly the Ginza Rabba.
sections.spread:
Perkins divides the development of Gnosticism into three periods. The mid-2nd to early 3rd century was the high point of the classical Gnostic teachers and their systems, and from the end of the 2nd century to the 4th a reaction by the proto-orthodox church and condemnation as heresy led to decline. The movement spread in areas controlled by the Roman Empire and Arian Goths, and the Persian Empire. Valentinianism spread to Northwest Africa and Egypt, and east to Asia Minor and Syria. Marcion's congregation, founded after he preached in Rome about 150, spread throughout the Mediterranean, though some scholars do not count him a Gnostic. Basilidianism was almost exclusively limited to Egypt and survived until the end of the 4th century.

Decline set in during the 3rd century because of the rise of proto-orthodoxy and the deterioration of the Roman Empire. After declining in the western Mediterranean, Gnosticism persisted in the Near East until at least the 6th century and remained influential as far as China until the late 9th. Ideas then resurfaced in groups such as the Paulicians, between 650 and 872 in Armenia, the Bogomils, who emerged in Bulgaria between 927 and 970, and the Cathars. Conversion to Islam and the Albigensian Crusade (1209–1229) greatly reduced the remaining numbers.
sections.community:
Gnostic groups were diverse and never formed a single church. Modern scholars distinguish a Judean–Israelite branch, including the Elkesaites, a baptismal group active between 100 and 400, and the Mandaeans; a Syriac–Egyptian one, including the Sethians, Valentinians, Basilidians and Serpent Gnostics; and a Persian one, including Manichaeism. Valentinus (c. 100 – c. 180) was a candidate for bishop of Rome but started his own group when another was chosen, and his school was popular, intellectually vibrant and numerous. Gnostic teachers and early Gnostic sects saw themselves as Christians.

The Church Fathers denounced Gnostic ideas as heresy, and efforts to destroy Gnostic texts were largely successful, so that very little writing by Gnostic thinkers survives. The Christian heresiologists accused some groups of libertine practice, among them the Cainites, the Carpocratians and the Borborites, but there is little evidence about the nature of the Cainites. Women in most Gnostic literature are portrayed as chaotic and disobedient, while the Nag Hammadi texts place women in roles of leadership and heroism, and some texts, such as the Gospel of Mary, treat Mary Magdalene as a leader superior to the twelve apostles. Neoplatonists such as Plotinus also opposed the Gnostics, rejecting their radical dualism.
sections.legacy:
Mandaeism is the only surviving Gnostic religion from antiquity. The Mandaeans are an ethnoreligious group who speak Mandaic, a dialect of Eastern Aramaic, and live in southern Iraq and the Iranian province of Khuzestan and in diaspora communities, with 60,000 to 70,000 worldwide. They revere John the Baptist and baptise repeatedly. Yezidism, originally practised in northern Mesopotamia, may also be regarded as a continuation of Sethianism and Ophitism. Gnostic ideas are also found in Islamic and Kabbalistic thought, though Scholem's claim of Cathar influence on Kabbalah has not been substantiated by extant texts, according to Dan Joseph.

Since 1890, when Jules Doinel re-established a Gnostic church in France, a number of modern Gnostic churches have been founded, among them the Ecclesia Gnostica and the Apostolic Johannite Church, many after the Nag Hammadi discovery. Thinkers such as Schopenhauer, Carl Jung, Hans Jonas and Harold Bloom studied or were influenced by Gnosticism. Since the 1990s scholars have debated whether it is a form of early Christianity, a category created by orthodox Christians, or a distinct tradition. Michael Williams proposed "Biblical-Demiurgic tradition" in 1996, and Karen King argued in 2004 that the term does injustice to the diversity of early Christianity.

summary: Gnosticism is a modern term for diverse religious systems of the 2nd century and after that stressed saving knowledge and set a hidden supreme being above a flawed creator. For centuries it was known mainly through its opponents, until the Nag Hammadi library was found in 1945. Mandaeism survives as its one ancient continuation.
references: David Brakke, The Gnostics: Myth, Ritual, and Diversity in Early Christianity (Harvard University Press, 2012)
Roelof van den Broek, Gnostic Religion in Antiquity (Cambridge University Press, 2013)
Hans Jonas, The Gnostic Religion (Beacon Press, 1963)
Karen L. King, What is Gnosticism? (Harvard University Press, 2003)
Kurt Rudolph, Gnosis: The Nature & History of Gnosticism (Harper & Row, 1987)
